item.title: Economy Overshadows GOP Border Success, Says Samara Klar
item.description:
Samara Klar, professor at the University of Arizona School of Government and Public Policy, said that high prices are dragging Republican messaging in Arizona ahead of President Trump's visit to campaign in the state. Klar also spoke about the how the issue of immigration enforcement and border security is playing alongside affordability. She said that Republicans might not be able to capitalize on border wins as 'the economy is such an issue for voters that in many ways it’s overshadowing a lot of the successes Republicans might have otherwise been able to claim when it comes to border security.' (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: US, Chinese Robotaxi Rivals Race for Europe

Europe is emerging as a key battleground for the global robotaxi industry as US and Chinese companies look to expand autonomous driving beyond their home markets. Frank McCleary, a partner at Arthur D. Little, discusses Europe’s fragmented but evolving regulatory landscape, why Chinese operators see an opportunity there as the US remains largely closed to them, and whether experience gained deploying autonomous vehicles in China translates to cities overseas. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:

CEO Erik Bernhardsson discusses the company’s more than 3 billion AI sandboxes, growing demand for inference and reinforcement learning, and why increasingly capable agents will need secure virtual environments where they can execute code and eventually take on longer-running tasks. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Fed Weighs More Hikes on Inflation Concerns
item.description:
Barclays senior US economist Pooja Sriram said higher interest rates are a blunt tool that tighten financial conditions and hit rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and autos first. While rising Treasury yields and the bond selloff have added restraint, she said it is unclear whether conditions are restrictive enough. With oil prices rising again, further pressure on housing and auto demand could create uneven economic damage without resolving inflation. Sriram said the Fed’s approach, reflected in September meeting minutes, is focused on managing the risk that strong demand, persistent inflation or adverse supply shocks push prices higher. The Fed appears prepared to raise rates further, though she said a hike as soon as October is unlikely. (Source: Bloomberg)

He highlighted growing demand for frontier models like Opus 5.5, now about 40% cheaper than its predecessor, and a shift toward using different models for specific tasks across the 5.5 family. Princen emphasized Anthropic’s safety-first approach versus open-source and open-weight competitors, underscoring third-party auditing, closer cooperation with governments, and willingness to delay or limit powerful model releases—such as with Methos—if safety concerns arise, even at the expense of near-term revenue. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, ASML says supply won't meet demand for its chipmaking machines out to 2028. Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang has announced plans to invest $2 billion in European deals during a tour of the region. And Saudi Aramco’s executive headquarters in eastern Saudi Arabia was hit during a missile attack by Houthi militants. On today's show, attacks over the weekend in Saudi Arabia in which 13 people were killed risk widening the conflict in the Middle East. An American was among those killed on Saturday, raising pressure for US President Donald Trump to act. Oil extended losses as traders assessed President Trump's announcement of an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine. And the EU has announced a cap of 350,000 on imports of Chinese hybrid cars following talks between trade chief Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: How AI Is Upending the World of Mathematics
item.description:
Last month, OpenAI announced that it had produced an AI-generated proof for the Navier-Stokes problem. LLMs used to be bad at counting, but now they are solving math problems that have stumped humans for decades. Meanwhile, at universities, the problem of AI in education continues: Now that LLMs can do a student's homework, teachers are struggling to keep up. It is clear that AI is very quickly changing how math is taught and how it is practiced by professionals. Justin Solomon, who is the associate dean for engineering education at MIT, gives us a primer on how mathematicians (both pure and applied) are responding to all the advances in AI. He also explains what exactly the Navier-Stokes problem is and why the OpenAI proof is hard for even the pros to parse, what movies get wrong about how mathematicians do their jobs, and how he's changing his pedagogical approach in the age of AI. (Source: Bloomberg)

In this episode of Power On, Mark Gurman and Bloomberg tech editor Vlad Savov unpack John Ternus’ first month running Apple — from his push to make the company leaner and faster to his unusually hands-on role overseeing design. They discuss why more layoffs could be coming, how Ternus is putting design back at the center of Apple and why Tim Cook, now executive chairman, remains the company’s face on the world stage. Then, Mark gives his verdict on Meta’s new $1,299 VR glasses after trying them himself — and explains why they are the device Apple’s Vision Pro should have been all along. Have a question for Mark? But according to the economist and policy analyst Dominik Leusder (who also writes the Leusder of Last Resort Substack) the Draghi report might have mismeasured the true scale of Europe's issues, and he asks if the popular narrative of European decline is an accurate one. We also speak about whether Europe needs a frontier AI model, why long, wine-soaked lunches are not a good way to measure productivity, and the state of Europe's vexed relationship with China as a trade partner and competitor. item.title: Why Treasuries Are ‘Risky’ Again
item.description:
We all know that Treasury yields have been surging, alongside bond yields all around the world. So what explains the selloff and does it mean that bonds are becoming fundamentally riskier? What happens if investors can no longer hedge stocks with government debt? And how do expectations of the Federal Reserve's "reaction function" fit in? In this episode, we speak with Carolin Pflueger, associate professor at the University of Chicago and a resident scholar at the Chicago Fed, about her work on the bond market and central banks. We discuss why bonds have become more stock-like, what that means for yields, and the role of the Fed's credibility in making bonds “bond-like” again. (Source: Bloomberg)

(FICO) shares are rising after the company launched the FICO Mortgage Direct License Program, and Bill Pulte signaled he wasn't purposefully targeting the company, which may have contributed to the stock's rise on Thursday. (Source: Bloomberg)

Myriad forces have combined to push the government’s borrowing costs higher — from $100-a-barrel oil and the AI spending boom, to yawning US budget deficits adding to a record $40 trillion debt load — all against a backdrop of a Federal Reserve bent on cooling inflation that’s run well past target for years. The selling pressure intensified this week as energy prices surged anew and data showed US businesses are humming along, giving an already hawkish central bank more reasons to keep raising interest rates.
